title: Revolut's Swiss FINMA bid and what AI banking agents mean for AML
summary: Revolut applies for a Swiss banking licence while deploying AI agents reshape AML obligations across fintech. Plus: Malaysia's MyPDP tender, the HKMA self-assessment deadline, and what a 47 million Australian dollar DCE penalty signals for tranche two readiness.
script:
ALEX: Let me put a pattern on the table before we get into individual stories today. Three of the items in front of us, Revolut's FINMA application, Zopa's AI banking agent rollout, and Malaysia's personal data protection platform tender, all point to the same underlying tension. Regulated obligations are expanding faster than compliance infrastructure is being built to support them. Jordan, is that the right frame?

JORDAN: Partially. I'd sharpen it. It's not just that obligations are expanding. It's that the firms driving the expansion are actively choosing to expand them, by applying for new licences, by deploying new customer-facing technology, by moving into new product lines. And they're doing that while their AML frameworks are still catching up to the last expansion. That's the part that should make MLROs uncomfortable. This is AML Agents Briefing for Thursday the eighteenth of September 2026.

ALEX: So let's start with Revolut, because this is the most straightforward compliance story of the day. Revolut has secured a banking licence in Colombia and simultaneously filed a formal application with FINMA, Switzerland's Financial Market Supervisory Authority, for a Swiss banking authorisation. Two jurisdictions, two separate regulatory regimes, two separate AML/CFT frameworks, effectively in parallel.

JORDAN: And I want to push back on the word "simultaneously" slightly, because I think it flatters the sequencing. When you're filing for a Swiss banking licence, FINMA's AML expectations are not a checkbox at the end of the process. Swiss banking authorisation requires demonstrating a fully operational anti-money-laundering framework that meets FINMA's Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance requirements before the licence is granted. The question I'd be asking if I were Revolut's group MLRO is whether the resourcing for both of these authorisations is genuinely parallel or whether one jurisdiction is getting the attention and the other is getting a template.

ALEX: That's fair, and it connects to a broader supervisory pattern. FINMA has been notably more assertive on AML governance since its 2023 thematic review of fintech firms. An application from a firm of Revolut's scale and complexity is not going to get a light-touch examination.

JORDAN: Right. And for our listeners who are compliance heads at other fintechs watching this, the read-across is straightforward. If you are managing AML obligations across more than two jurisdictions, and especially if you are in the middle of any licence expansion, now is the time to do an honest mapping exercise. Which jurisdictions have a fully documented, locally tested AML framework, and which ones are running on a group policy that hasn't been localised. FINMA will find the gap. So will BNM. So will AUSTRAC.

ALEX: Moving on, let's spend a moment on Zopa's AI agent deployment, because I think this is the story that's going to feel like customer-experience news but is actually a compliance architecture question.

JORDAN: It absolutely is. Zopa Bank has begun rolling out a conversational AI agent to current account holders. And the compliance issue isn't the AI itself. It's what the AI does when a customer says something that would, if a human heard it, trigger a suspicion report. Does the AI flag it? Does it capture it? Does it route it? Does anyone in the MLRO's team even know what the AI is logging?

ALEX: And I'd go further than that. Under the UK's Proceeds of Crime Act, the tipping-off provisions apply regardless of the channel through which a suspicious disclosure is made. If an AI agent is the first point of contact and it doesn't have a defined escalation path to the MLRO, you have a structural gap in your suspicious transaction reporting framework.

JORDAN: That's the point exactly. And while Zopa is a UK firm, this isn't a UK-only issue. Any APAC digital bank or electronic money institution deploying conversational AI to customers needs to ask the same question. MAS Notice 626 on anti-money-laundering for banks doesn't carve out AI-generated customer interactions. Your suspicious transaction reporting obligations apply to every channel.

ALEX: So what's the concrete action for listeners here?

JORDAN: If you're the MLRO at a digital bank or a firm that has deployed or is piloting any form of conversational AI for customers, this week you need to sit down with your technology team and your vendor and get a written answer to three specific questions. First, what customer inputs does the AI log and for how long. Second, is there any automated flagging if a customer's input contains typology indicators. Third, what is the escalation path from the AI layer to the MLRO's team. If you don't have written answers to all three, you have a gap that an examiner will find.

ALEX: Shifting our focus, briefly, to Malaysia. The Department of Personal Data Protection, known as JPDP, published a public tender on the seventeenth of September, posted to the department's website at pdp.gov.my, for the development of what they're calling MyPDP, an integrated platform to operationalise amendments to the Personal Data Protection Act 2010, which is Act 709.

JORDAN: Now this sits slightly adjacent to pure AML, but it matters for financial crime compliance in one specific way. The amended PDPA changes the data-handling obligations around customer information, and that intersects directly with how firms manage KYC records, how they share customer data with group entities for consolidated monitoring, and whether their data retention policies remain compliant under both the amended PDPA and their AML record-keeping obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001.

ALEX: Do you think most compliance teams in Malaysia have mapped that intersection?

JORDAN: Honestly? No. I think most firms have their data protection team handling the PDPA amendments and their AML team handling AMLA obligations, and the two are not talking to each other about where the frameworks overlap and, more importantly, where they conflict.

ALEX: That's the action item right there.

JORDAN: It is. If you're a compliance leader at a Malaysian financial institution, before the end of September, get your data protection officer and your MLRO in the same room and map the overlap. Specifically: your KYC record retention schedule, your intragroup data-sharing arrangements for transaction monitoring, and any automated profiling that touches customer personal data. The MyPDP platform isn't live yet, but the amended Act obligations are moving and firms need to be ahead of the implementation.

ALEX: Before we close, one obligation that is not hypothetical. The HKMA's annual self-assessment return under its AML/CFT Guideline Section 11 is due on the thirtieth of September. That's twelve days away. The return covers the 2024 reporting period and requires independent validation by Internal Audit before submission via the HKMA's prescribed Excel template.

JORDAN: If your Internal Audit sign-off isn't already in hand, it should be your first call this morning. Late submission isn't just an administrative inconvenience under HKMA's framework. It's a supervisory relationship event.

ALEX: And on the horizon, the forty-seven million Australian dollar civil penalty that AUSTRAC imposed against a registered digital currency exchange for systemic transaction monitoring failures continues to resonate. The full findings are on austrac.gov.au. If you're running AML/CTF compliance at any Australian reporting entity, and particularly any tranche-two entity preparing for obligations coming into force, that penalty is required reading for your next risk committee discussion.

JORDAN: The three failure categories in that penalty, transaction monitoring, mule-account detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness, are exactly the three areas AUSTRAC's supervisory teams are going to examine first in tranche-two inspections. Don't wait to be asked.

ALEX: Full source links and the obligation register are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. Jordan, last word?

JORDAN: The firms expanding fastest right now are the ones whose compliance teams most need more time and resource, not less. If any of what we've covered today felt uncomfortably close to your own pipeline, use that discomfort productively. See you tomorrow.
